title: Pirate Radio: Mavericks on the High Seas
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the British pirate radio boom of the 1960s, centered on Ronan O'Reilly's Radio Caroline, which broadcast rock and roll from ships in international waters beyond BBC and UK government control. They cover the rival Radio Atlanta, the DJs who worked the ships, the influence on psychedelia and British rock, the 1966-67 shooting incident involving Radio City that led to the Marine Broadcasting Offenses Act, and a brief look at Reverend Carl McIntyre's failed 1930s-era... (note: McIntyre's ship attempt), then turn to modern American pirate radio, New York FM pirate stations, and the 2020 PIRATE Act and FCC enforcement, with a closing listener mail about soap making in Senegal by Peace Corps volunteer Gracie Nagel.

segments.title: Book pre-order plug and show intro
segments.summary: Josh promotes the pre-order of the Stuff You Should Know book, then opens the episode with banter about the movie Pump Up the Volume and Sound Garden.

segments.title: Introduction to British pirate radio and the BBC monopoly
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the 1960s British pirate radio invasion and contrast the UK's government-controlled broadcasting with the more open US radio spectrum. They describe the BBC's refusal to play rock and roll and the limited options such as Radio Luxembourg.

segments.title: Ronan O'Reilly, Radio Caroline and Radio Atlanta
segments.summary: Ronan O'Reilly exploited the three-mile limit beyond UK jurisdiction to launch Radio Caroline from a ship, inspired by Scandinavian pirate stations. Rival Alan Crawford's Radio Atlanta raced to launch, and the ships were renamed after Caroline Kennedy and Atlanta.

segments.title: Radio Caroline's format, launch and influence on music
segments.summary: Radio Caroline launched around Easter 1964 with a rock format, quickly drew a larger audience than the BBC stations combined, and merged with Radio Atlanta. Its influence on psychedelia and bands like the Moody Blues is discussed, and the term pirate radio stuck from the start.

segments.title: Pirate DJs, listener fandom and the word anorak
segments.summary: Tony Blackburn, Emperor Roscoe (Mike Pasternak), Pete Tong and Andy Archer are discussed as DJs of the pirate ships. Andy Archer is credited with coining anorak for obsessive fans who hired boats to visit the ships. The DJs were largely professionals, with limited beer rations.

segments.title: Radio City shooting and Marine Broadcasting Offenses Act
segments.summary: A dispute between Radio City's Lord Smedley and REDG. Calvert over a transmitter led to a shooting at Calvert's home, with Smedley acquitted on self-defense grounds. The incident helped prompt the UK government to pass the Marine Broadcasting Offenses Act, justified publicly by distress-signal interference concerns.

segments.title: Ship fates, George Harrison and Radio Caroline museum
segments.summary: O'Reilly kept Radio Caroline going after his ship was seized by Dutch authorities; George Harrison and Tom Jones reportedly helped fund it. The Mi Amigo ran aground and sank; the Ross Revenge replaced it and was planned as a museum.

segments.title: Hosts' travel plans and personal ancestry banter
segments.summary: The hosts discuss future travel plans to the UK, New Zealand, Canada, and Germany, and briefly share their DNA ancestry results.

segments.title: Reverend Carl McIntyre and early US pirate broadcasting
segments.summary: The hosts describe the US pirate radio history, including the 1930s-era RXK station off Long Beach and Reverend Carl McIntyre's brief ship broadcast, which was shut down after ten hours. McIntyre had earlier been pushed off stations by the fairness doctrine, and a correction is given that the boat smoked rather than caught fire.

segments.title: Modern US pirate radio, New York and the PIRATE Act
segments.summary: Pirate radio persists in US cities, especially New York and Brooklyn, often serving immigrant and underserved communities in their native languages. The FCC has stepped up enforcement, and the PIRATE Act raised maximum fines to two million dollars. The hosts argue the law is aimed at intimidation and favors licensed broadcasters, while noting pirate stations rarely interfere with other signals and would also carry emergency information.

segments.title: Listener mail: soap making in Senegal
segments.summary: A listener, Gracie Nagel, describes training women's groups in Senegal as a Peace Corps volunteer to make and sell soap. The hosts thank her and invite listeners to send in their own good deeds.
